title: THE MOST TERRIFYING WORDS JESUS EVER SPOKE TO RELIGIOUS PEOPLE: “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
paragraphs: THE MOST TERRIFYING WORDS JESUS EVER SPOKE TO RELIGIOUS PEOPLE: “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”

They called Him Lord. They performed miracles in His name. They believed they belonged to Him. But when eternity arrived, Jesus said something they never imagined hearing. Could the same warning be speaking to the Church today?
Not because Jesus was trying to frighten sincere believers away from Him.
Not because His mercy has limits that a repentant sinner cannot cross.
But because He described people who were absolutely convinced they belonged to Him.
They knew His name.
They spoke His name.
They did extraordinary things in His name.
And somehow, through all their religious activity, they had missed the very One they claimed to serve.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.
No more Sundays. No more sermons. No more opportunities to hide behind appearances. No more carefully constructed image of who you want people to believe you are.
Just you.
And the Savior who knows everything.
You open your mouth, expecting to be welcomed.
“Lord, Lord…”
But before you can finish defending your life, you hear words that shatter every assumption you ever made about your faith.
“I never knew you.”
Not “I used to know you.”
Not “You weren't religious enough.”
Not “You didn't accomplish enough for My kingdom.”
“I never knew you.”
And suddenly, the most frightening possibility in the world is no longer that people might discover who you really are.
It is that you might have spent your entire life knowing about Jesus without ever truly belonging to Him.
This is not a fictional warning invented to provoke emotion.
These are the words of Jesus Himself.
In Matthew 7:21–23, during the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus declares:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
— Matthew 7:21–23, King James Version
Read that again, especially the word many.
Jesus did not say that nobody would be deceived about their relationship with Him.
He said many would stand before Him claiming spiritual credentials that could not save them.
And what makes this warning so unsettling is who these people appear to be.
They are not presented as people who openly despised Jesus.
They call Him Lord.
They claim to have prophesied in His name.
They claim to have cast out demons in His name.
They claim to have performed mighty works in His name.
Their argument is not that Jesus is irrelevant.
Their argument is that their religious accomplishments should prove they belong to Him.
Yet Jesus rejects that argument completely.
Why?
Because the kingdom of heaven is not entered through religious performance.
And calling Jesus Lord is not the same as surrendering to His lordship.
There is something in the original Greek that makes this passage even more piercing.
When Jesus says, “I never knew you,” Matthew records:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
The words mean, “I never knew you.”
The Greek word oudépote means “never” or “not ever.” The verb egnōn comes from ginōskō, meaning “to know.”
In this context, Jesus is not saying He lacked information about these people.
That would contradict the biblical testimony that God knows the human heart.
He is denying that they belonged to Him in the saving relationship they claimed to possess.
Jesus knew their names.
He knew their actions.
He knew their secrets.
But they were not His.
That distinction should disturb our spiritual complacency.
Because you can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
You can defend biblical doctrines while refusing to obey the One those doctrines reveal.
You can memorize Scripture and still resist its authority over your life.
You can appear spiritually mature in public while privately nurturing sins you have no intention of surrendering.
You can build a reputation around Jesus while your heart remains far from Him.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility of all is this:
You can become so accustomed to looking like a Christian that you stop asking whether you are actually following Christ.
But before anyone begins to despair, we must understand something essential.
Jesus did not give this warning so that every struggling believer would live in terror of being rejected.
He gave it to expose false confidence and call people toward genuine faith.
There is a difference between a person who struggles against sin and a person who has made peace with sin.
There is a difference between someone who falls and returns to Christ in repentance and someone who uses religious language to excuse a life of deliberate rebellion.
There is a difference between a wounded disciple crying, “Lord, help me,” and an unrepentant heart insisting, “Lord, look at everything I have done.”
The difference is not sinless perfection.
The difference is the reality of faith, repentance, and a life being transformed by grace.
And this is where the warning becomes deeply personal.
What if Jesus is not asking you to count how many Christian things you have done?
What if He is confronting the question you have been avoiding?
Have you truly surrendered your life to Me?
Perhaps you grew up in church.
You learned the songs before you understood their meaning.
You knew when to stand, when to bow your head, when to say amen.
You were baptized.
You attended Bible studies.
You served in ministry.
People looked at you and saw someone who had everything together spiritually.
But behind the familiar religious routine, something was missing.
You prayed when you needed something, but rarely sought God simply because you loved Him.
You read Scripture when you needed encouragement, but avoided the passages that confronted your behavior.
You wanted Jesus to rescue you from consequences, but you resisted Him when He called you to abandon the sin causing them.
You wanted His peace without His correction.
His promises without His commands.
His forgiveness without repentance.
His kingdom without His kingship.
And little by little, Christianity became something you performed rather than a life surrendered to Christ.
If that description touches something uncomfortable inside you, do not immediately push it away.
Sometimes the mercy of God reaches us through a truth we would rather not hear.
Because the warning that exposes false security can also become the invitation that leads us to genuine salvation.
Notice what Jesus says in Matthew 7:21.
The one who enters the kingdom is the one who does the will of His Father in heaven.
The Greek expression is:
ὁ ποιῶν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός μου
Ho poiōn to thelēma tou patros mou.
It refers to the one doing the will of My Father.
But we must be careful not to twist this into the idea that human obedience earns salvation.
Scripture does not teach that sinners can work their way into heaven.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And the very next verse, Ephesians 2:10, explains that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because our good works have purchased God's acceptance.
We are saved by grace through faith, and that grace produces a changed life.
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase salvation.
It is the fruit of a faith that truly belongs to Jesus.
Even the will of the Father must be understood through the whole testimony of Scripture.
In John 6:40, Jesus identifies the Father's will with looking to the Son and believing in Him for eternal life.
And in Matthew 7, He exposes the emptiness of religious claims that are disconnected from genuine submission to God.
Faith and obedience are not competing paths to salvation.
True faith receives Christ, and the Christ who saves us also begins transforming us.
That transformation may be slow.
It may involve painful struggles.
It may include tears, setbacks, confession, correction, and the daily need for mercy.
But genuine grace does not teach us to embrace the darkness from which Christ came to rescue us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings salvation and teaches us to walk in newness of life.
And here is where the story becomes even more astonishing.
The people in Matthew 7 point to what they have done.
“Have we not prophesied?”
“Have we not cast out devils?”
“Have we not done many wonderful works?”
Listen to the repeated emphasis.
We.
We.
We.
Their defense is built around their accomplishments.
But nobody enters the kingdom because their spiritual résumé is impressive enough to outweigh their sin.
Our hope is not found in presenting Jesus with a list of achievements.
Our hope is found in Jesus Himself.
His perfect obedience.
His sacrificial death.
His victorious resurrection.
His righteousness received through faith.
His mercy toward sinners who cannot save themselves.
That is why the Gospel is so much more beautiful than religious self-confidence.
Religion, when reduced to self-salvation, says, “Look what I have done.”
The Gospel says, “Look what Jesus has done.”
And there is a moment elsewhere in Scripture that makes the contrast almost unbearable.
Think about Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had confessed that Jesus was the Christ.
He had boldly declared that he would never abandon Him.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied even knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Luke 22:61 tells us that after Peter's denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
Imagine that look.
Peter had just denied the Savior who loved him.
And now their eyes met.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
His confidence had collapsed.
His courage had failed.
His promises had broken.
If salvation depended on an impressive record of spiritual consistency, what hope would Peter have had?
But Peter's story did not end in the courtyard.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter, as recorded in John 21.
Three times Jesus asked him about his love.
And the man who had denied his Lord was entrusted with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter was not restored because his failure had been insignificant.
He was restored because Jesus is merciful, and His grace is greater than the failure of a repentant disciple.
Now compare Peter's brokenness with the confidence of the people in Matthew 7.
Peter wept over his sin.
They defended themselves with their accomplishments.
Peter had nothing left to boast about.
They stood before Jesus listing reasons they deserved acceptance.
Peter's hope was the Savior who restored him.
Their argument was the ministry they claimed to have performed.
This is not a declaration that tears automatically prove salvation, or that every religious accomplishment is false.
It is a reminder that a humbled sinner clinging to Christ is in a far better position than a self-assured religious person who sees no need to repent.
And perhaps someone reading this has been living with the quiet fear that they have failed God too many times.
You know the temptation you keep fighting.
You remember the words you wish you could take back.
You carry shame from decisions nobody else knows about.
You wonder whether Jesus could still welcome you after everything.
Listen carefully.
The same Jesus who warned about false disciples also promised in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
That promise matters.
The invitation is real.
The mercy is real.
The forgiveness is real.
And no repentant sinner needs to imagine that Christ is reluctant to receive those who genuinely come to Him.
The cross was not built for people who could prove they never needed forgiveness.
Christ died for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love for us while we were still sinners.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the appearance of religious people.
He came to save the lost.
But His mercy must never be confused with indifference toward sin.
The Savior who forgave the guilty also called people to repentance.
The One who welcomed sinners did not teach them to remain comfortable in their bondage.
His grace is not a costume we wear over an unchanged heart.
It is the undeserved mercy of God that brings us into a new relationship with Him.
That is why Jesus' warning is especially important in an age when faith can become a public image.
We can post Bible verses while privately refusing to forgive.
We can share worship songs while cultivating bitterness.
We can argue passionately about biblical truth while treating people with cruelty.
We can accumulate followers by speaking about Jesus while neglecting the quiet obedience He commands when nobody is watching.
And yes, even Christian content creators, pastors, ministry leaders, and people who spend their lives publicly speaking about God must take this warning seriously.
A platform is not proof of spiritual maturity.
A large audience is not proof of God's approval.
Emotional reactions are not proof that a message is faithful to Scripture.
And even visible ministry results cannot replace the necessity of genuinely belonging to Christ.
This warning reaches the person behind the pulpit as surely as the person sitting in the last row.
It reaches the one writing this article as surely as the one reading it.
None of us is above the need to examine ourselves in the light of God's Word.
Second Corinthians 13:5 calls believers to examine whether they are in the faith.
Not to become trapped in endless self-condemnation.
Not to obsess over whether every weakness means they are lost.
But to refuse the dangerous comfort of a faith that exists only in name.
Ask yourself something.
When God's Word exposes your sin, what happens inside you?
Do you begin making excuses?
Do you search for someone whose failures appear worse?
Do you hide behind your church attendance, your giving, your service, or your reputation?
Or do you come before Jesus and admit that you need His mercy?
When the Holy Spirit brings conviction through Scripture, the right response is not to perform harder so that God will be impressed.
It is to repent, believe the Gospel, and walk in the grace that teaches us to obey.
And that brings us to another detail in Matthew 7 that is easy to miss.
Jesus says:
“Depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
The Greek expression includes:
οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν
Hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian.
This describes those who practice lawlessness.
The word anomía carries the sense of lawlessness or disregard for God's law.
Jesus is exposing a contradiction between their public profession and their actual lives.
They call Him Lord, yet their conduct is characterized by lawlessness.
They claim His authority while refusing to live under it.
Their problem is not that they were imperfect human beings who needed grace.
Their problem is that their religious claims concealed a fundamental refusal to submit to God.
And Jesus had already warned about this contradiction.
In Luke 6:46, He asks:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
That question cuts through centuries of religious appearances.
Why call Him Lord if His words carry no authority over your choices?
Why call Him Savior while insisting that the sins He died to redeem you from must remain untouched?
Why ask Him to direct your life while refusing to surrender the areas where His direction conflicts with your desires?
None of this means Christians become instantly perfect.
First John 1:8 warns against claiming to be without sin.
And First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess their sins.
The Christian life is not the absence of struggle.
It is a life of repentance, faith, dependence, and transformation under the grace of God.
A believer may stumble terribly.
But stumbling is not the same as declaring that God's commands no longer matter.
A believer may battle temptation repeatedly.
But battling sin is not the same as celebrating it.
A believer may need correction.
But receiving correction is part of learning to follow the Shepherd.
Jesus is not looking for people who have manufactured flawless lives.
He is calling people to belong to Him truly.
And now, perhaps, the most important question in this entire article is not whether you have ever said, “Lord, Lord.”
It is whether you have come to the Lord in repentance and faith.
Because there is a terrible difference between using the name of Jesus and trusting the person of Jesus.
You can invoke His name for success.
You can use His name to gain influence.
You can attach His name to your ambitions.
You can even use His name to persuade others that you are spiritually trustworthy.
But the question remains.
Is Jesus your Savior and Lord, or has He become a name you attach to a life you still insist on controlling?
That is a question worth sitting with.
Not for five seconds before scrolling to the next post.
Not until the discomfort disappears.
But long enough to let the truth confront whatever you have been protecting.
Maybe there is someone you need to forgive.
Maybe there is dishonesty you need to confess.
Maybe there is a relationship you need to bring under God's Word.
Maybe there is a hidden habit you have been excusing.
Maybe you have been serving in ministry while neglecting prayer, repentance, and your own walk with Christ.
Maybe you have spent years trying to convince everyone else that you are spiritually healthy while quietly feeling distant from God.
You do not need to pretend before the One who already knows you completely.
You can come into the light.
You can tell the truth.
You can stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
And you can turn to Christ today.
Not because an emotional article has the power to save you.
Not because commenting a prayer will earn forgiveness.
Not because giving money to a ministry will purchase your entrance into heaven.
But because Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose from the dead, and calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Mark 1:15 records His proclamation:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia), a word associated with a change of mind, expressed in a genuine turning toward God.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because you were caught.
It is not simply fearing consequences.
It is turning away from sin and toward God, trusting His mercy and receiving His authority over your life.
And even repentance must not become another achievement we boast about.
We come to God as needy sinners, dependent upon His grace.
The Gospel does not say, “Make yourself worthy, and then Jesus will receive you.”
It announces that Jesus is the only Savior who can reconcile the unworthy to God.
That is the wonder of the cross.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can be cleansed.
The rebellious can be reconciled.
The spiritually dead can be made alive in Christ.
The person who has spent years hiding behind religious appearances can finally stop pretending.
And the person who has wandered far from God can hear the call to return.
This is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is not simply a memorable phrase.
It is a declaration of what the Gospel makes possible.
Not that our sins were imaginary.
Not that our past actions carry no consequences.
Not that every broken relationship will automatically be restored.
But that our failures do not have to be the final word over our lives when we come to Christ.
Peter's denial was real.
His tears were real.
Christ's resurrection was real.
And his restoration was real.
The scandal of sin met the mercy of the risen Savior.
And the man who once denied Jesus became a witness to His grace.
That does not mean every story will unfold in the same way.
But it means no one needs to believe that their past is stronger than the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
Now imagine something different from the opening scene.
Imagine reaching the end of your earthly life, not carrying a résumé of religious achievements as your defense, but resting in the finished work of Christ.
Not saying, “Jesus, look how impressive I was.”
But trusting the Savior who died and rose again.
Not trusting your church attendance, your donations, your ministry position, or your reputation.
But trusting Christ alone.
And because you belong to Him, your life has increasingly reflected His grace through repentance, love, faith, and obedience.
That is the hope Jesus calls us toward.
Not the fragile confidence of spiritual performance.
But the living assurance of knowing Him and being known by Him.
Jesus says in John 10:27–28:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.”
Do you see the contrast?
In Matthew 7, Jesus says, “I never knew you.”
In John 10, Jesus says, “I know them.”
And His sheep hear His voice and follow Him.
Their security is not in their ability to save themselves.
Their security is in the Shepherd who gives eternal life.
What a difference it makes to belong to Him.
So today, do not merely ask whether you can remember the day you first called Jesus Lord.
Ask whether you are trusting Him now.
Do not merely ask whether other Christians think you are faithful.
Ask whether your life is being shaped by His Word.
Do not merely ask whether you have done something impressive in His name.
Ask whether you love the Christ whose name you proclaim.
And if the answer exposes a painful truth, do not run away from Him.
Run toward Him.
There is no safer place for a repentant sinner than the mercy of Jesus Christ.
You can pray honestly, even if your words are trembling.

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too much time trying to look faithful while hiding the places where I have resisted You. I cannot save myself. Forgive my sins. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You, turn from what dishonors You, and follow You with a sincere heart. Strip away my false confidence. Let my hope rest in Your grace, not my achievements. Change me by Your Spirit. I want to know You, not merely speak about You. Amen.”
Those words are not a magical formula.
What matters is the Savior to whom you turn in genuine repentance and faith.
And if you are already following Christ but have been wounded, discouraged, or exhausted by your struggles, remember this.
Conviction should lead you back to Jesus, not into hopelessness.
You do not need to earn your way back into His mercy through self-punishment.
Confess your sin.
Receive His forgiveness.
Seek the help of mature believers.
Return to His Word.
Continue following Him.
The God who calls His people to holiness also supplies grace for their growth.
And sometimes that growth begins with the courage to admit, “I need help.”
If this message has uncovered something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.
You do not need to disclose private sins or painful details publicly. God already knows your heart, and genuine repentance does not require a public performance.
But your honest response may remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who knows Christian language but may have never understood the difference between religious activity and saving faith.
Somewhere is a believer who thinks their repeated failures have placed them beyond the mercy of Christ.
Somewhere is a friend who has stopped attending church because they feel too ashamed to return.
Somewhere is a family member who desperately needs to hear that salvation is not purchased by good works, but received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Not to collect reactions.
Not to prove that you are more spiritual than anyone else.
But because Scripture's warning and the Gospel's promise deserve to be heard.
There may come a day when your heart needs to remember that Jesus calls us beyond religious appearances into a genuine relationship with Him.
There may come a day when someone asks you why good works cannot save us, or whether a struggling Christian can still have hope.
Let these Scriptures bring you back to the truth.
Our desire is not simply to publish messages that move people for a moment.
It is to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and keep their eyes on Jesus Christ long after the emotion of a single article has faded.

Every article takes time to study, write, examine, and prepare. Every resource shared represents an opportunity to help someone discover biblical truth. Every step toward reaching more readers requires continued effort and support.
Most importantly, it does not purchase God's favor, forgiveness, blessing, or salvation.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a promise that money can unlock spiritual blessings.
But willing generosity, rooted in gratitude to Christ and a desire to see His truth reach more people.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their faith, grow in biblical understanding, and deepen their walk with Jesus Christ.
Even if you are unable to give financially, you can still make a meaningful difference.
Invite someone to read it.
Pray for the people who will encounter it.
A prayer can express our dependence on the God who alone gives spiritual growth.
And none of those things should ever become substitutes for personally knowing Jesus Christ.

Because when all the ministry activities are finished, when every article has been written, when every audience has moved on, and when every earthly achievement has faded, only one question will finally matter.
Do you belong to Jesus?
Not merely to a church.
Not merely to a Christian community.
Not merely to a ministry.
Not merely to a tradition.
To Jesus.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who knows the secrets of every heart.
The One who exposes empty religion.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who saves by grace.
The One who calls His people to follow Him.
And the One before whom every human being will ultimately stand.
The warning of Matthew 7 is too serious to ignore.
But the mercy of Jesus is too wonderful to overlook.
So do not spend your life trying to impress the Savior you have been invited to trust.
Do not hide behind spiritual accomplishments when He is calling you to repentance.
Do not confuse knowing the language of Christianity with knowing Christ Himself.
Come to Him.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
And let the Gospel transform what religious appearances never could.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be reaching the end of your life without having impressed the world.
It would be spending your whole life saying His name while refusing to come to the One who could have saved you.
